en: The Sūtra on the Parable of the Herd of Cows, translated by the Śramaṇa Faju of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Suppose there were a herd of oxen, well-tamed and gentle by nature; wherever they went, they would select soft grass to eat and drink cool, clear water."
At that time, there was a donkey who thought to himself:
"These herds of oxen are gentle and well-trained by nature; wherever they go, they select soft grass to eat and drink cool, clear water."
"I too shall now imitate them: I will choose soft grass to eat and drink cool, clear water.
Then that donkey joined the herd of oxen; he kicked up the earth with his forefeet to harass the herd, and he even imitated the bellowing of the oxen, yet he could not change his own voice:
"I am an ox too! I am an ox too!"
"Yet those cattle, having gored him with their horns, would kill him and depart, leaving him behind.
This case is just like that.
If there is a bhikṣu who is not diligent and cultivates unwholesome dharmas;"
Not being a śramaṇa, they claim to be a śramaṇa;
not practicing the holy life, they claim to practice the holy life;
furthermore, they are not of much learning and hold wrong views.
Their deportment was not complete—whether walking to and fro, bending and stretching, or looking up and down—they did not know how to properly put on their robes or carry their bowls;
they were unable to obtain clothing, bedding, food and drink, or medicinal requisites for treating illness and debility.
If he sees a bhikṣu who is diligent in cultivating wholesome dharmas, who has accomplished the conduct of a śramaṇa among śramaṇas,
who practices the brahma-faring,
and who, being widely learned and erudite, cultivates wholesome dharmas;

His deportment was entirely excellent; whether walking or coming and going, bending or stretching, looking down or looking up, putting on his robes or holding his alms bowl, he never failed in propriety;
and he obtained clothing, bedding, food and drink, seats and bedding, and medicine for the sick.
At that time, the bhikṣu of evil conduct thought to himself:

"These many bhikṣus are diligent and cultivate wholesome dharmas; they fulfill the conduct of a śramaṇa among śramaṇas and the conduct of a brahmacārin among brahmacārins. Their deportment is complete; their walking, coming and going, bending and stretching, bowing and looking up, wearing robes and carrying the alms-bowl—all are fully perfected.
They have obtained clothing, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for illness—all of which are already provided in abundance."
"I shall now enter among that assembly; there too I shall obtain robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicine for the sick.

At that time, an evil bhikṣu—one who practiced unwholesome dharmas, lacked the conduct of a śramaṇa yet claimed to be a śramaṇa, lacked the holy life (*brahmacarya*) yet claimed to practice it, was of little learning, and held various evil views—entered into the midst of those many bhikṣus who were diligent. Desiring to imitate their deportment and etiquette—their walking and coming and going, their bending and stretching, their looking up and down, and their wearing of robes and holding of the bowl—he acted exactly like those subtle and wondrous bhikṣus who were diligent, practiced wholesome dharmas, and walked, came and went, bent and stretched, looked up and down, wore their robes, and held their bowls.
Then he spoke these words: "I am a śramaṇa! I am a śramaṇa!"
At that time, the bhikṣu Subhānu fully realized and understood: "This bhikṣu is not diligent, yet he claims to be diligent;
he is not a śramaṇa, yet he claims to be a śramaṇa;
he does not cultivate the holy life, yet he claims to cultivate the holy life."
Lacking extensive learning and holding various wrong views, the subtle and refined bhikṣus then expelled him beyond the boundaries of the community, saying:
"Depart quickly; do not remain within our assembly."
"Just as those cattle, being well-tamed by nature, drive out that donkey,
so too, monks, you should abandon and distance yourselves from what is not the practice of a śramaṇa and what is not the practice of a brāhmaṇa."
The wholesome conduct of the śramaṇas and the wholesome conduct of the brāhmaṇas should be properly recited and maintained.
In this way, monks,
you should train yourselves.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
This concludes the *Sūtra of the Simile of the Herd of Cows* as taught by the Buddha.
